extracted.intended_audience: researchers in science communication, health/medical journalists, press officers and public relations professionals who write or evaluate press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for evaluating how cancer-genetics research is presented in press releases and in subsequent lay-press coverage, focusing on accuracy, language, qualifiers, and potential distortions introduced by intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid biologically deterministic portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories (and press releases) should not present genetics in biologically deterministic terms — i.e., implying genes alone determine complex health outcomes/behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract cites earlier studies reporting misrepresentation by presenting biologically deterministic and simplified portrayals; avoid phrasing that suggests a single gene 'causes' complex traits. Anti-patterns include deterministic language and headlines implying inevitability. Evaluate for presence/absence of deterministic claims and whether uncertainty or multifactorial causation is acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include qualifying details
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases and news coverage should provide qualifying details about the research (limitations, scope, effect sizes, populations, study design) rather than making unqualified claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study observes a lack of qualifying details as a common error attributed to science journalism and press releases. Guidance: report sample size, whether findings are correlational vs causal, magnitude of effects, and relevant caveats. Scoring can penalize omissions of basic qualifiers that contextualize claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid oversimplified language and misleading metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication should refrain from oversimplified labels or metaphors (e.g., 'fat gene') that obscure nuance and mislead lay audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract gives 'fat gene' as an example of oversimplified language. Prefer precise descriptors (e.g., 'variant associated with increased BMI in [population]'). Evaluate copy for reductive nicknames, catchy metaphors, or shorthand that misrepresents complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not imply causation from correlational findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports should not imply causal relationships between genes and behaviors/outcomes when the underlying research is correlational or does not establish causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the paper studies genetics related to cancer outcomes and behaviors (prostate, breast, colon cancer, smoking, obesity), watch for language that leaps from association to causation. Guidance: explicitly mark when findings are associations, describe potential confounders, and avoid policy/behavioral recommendations that presuppose causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the press release as a potential source of distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the press release itself introduces distortions, simplifications, or hype that are then propagated by lay-press coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study's findings suggest press releases — not solely news stories — may serve as the source of distortion. Guidance: compare press release claims to original research phrasing; check for added claims, omitted caveats, or sensationalized framing in the press release that could mislead subsequent coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider public health/lay audience impact
rubrics_metrics.description: When communicating genetic findings, account for the potential effects on public understanding and health-related behaviors; prioritize clarity and responsible framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract emphasizes that how discoveries are presented can have significant effects on health outcomes. Guidance: assess whether messaging could lead to misinformed health decisions, undue fear or complacency, or stigma; recommend inclusion of actionable, accurate context for lay readers.
